title: Judgment of Works and the Temple of God
english: …of Christ our God." If men cannot grasp the mind of God so as to know it, then they cannot know ours either, since we have the mind and wisdom of God.

On 1 Corinthians 3:1–3: Unbelievers are more ready to follow wonders. So I gave you a word, but not the perfect and hidden wisdom, the dispensation of the Passion, which only the mature among believers accept. He also uses "milk" as a figure for moral teaching and for coming to faith through signs, and "solid food" for the proclamation of divine doctrines. "Milk" can also mean the light commands: "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12), "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14), and the like, and "Come, follow me" (Matthew 19:21). Then, when he says, "You are fleshly and walk in a merely human way," he means: you honor what is human and do not seek the things of God.
On 1 Corinthians 3:5: That is, equal in their service.

On 1 Corinthians 3:6–10: Some of this he says in terms of farming, some in terms of building. He says that he himself planted, made the beginning, and laid the foundation of God's building. He charges those who build on the foundation after him not to treat the building as a side task. By "foundation" he means the faith and the preaching.

On 1 Corinthians 3:11–15: Christ is not called the foundation of creation, as the Arians falsely insist, but of the faith. Christ was preached, and the whole building rises on this foundation. Those who teach preach one faith and proclaim the life of the gospel; it is up to us to make ourselves precious stones, or wood, hay or straw. So when he says, "Let each one take care how he builds on it," what can that refer to if not to how we live? "For no one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid." The teacher proclaims Christ and passes on his commands; the rest is to become like gold through purity, or like hay through weakness. So when he charges, "Let each one take care," and what follows, he is addressing those who wanted to be named after the men who baptized or taught them. "If anyone's work that he has built on it remains": you see that the builder builds something good. But sometimes it does not remain, because the will has changed for the worse. "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire." The words are out of their natural order. It should be read: "If anyone's work is burned up, it will suffer loss, yet so as through fire," meaning that it will be burned up and suffer loss as through fire, "but he himself will be saved," for the turn for the worse did not happen through him.

This is said with the words out of their natural order, so that it runs: "If anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward, and he himself will be saved. If anyone's work is burned, it will suffer loss and be burned as through fire." But how will he himself be saved if the work he built is burned up? "Yet so as through fire": he will be judged on whether he left out anything that served to correct sinners or to warn them, as in Ezekiel.

On 1 Corinthians 3:16–18: He turns again to those who trust in their own wisdom. He calls believers temples of God, and he says that those who trust in eloquence destroy the temple of God, as the next words will show: "If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool." Why, then, does someone who trusts in outside wisdom destroy the temple? If you are God's temple, you ought to have him as your teacher and revealer. But if you leave the one who dwells in you and rely on your own intelligence, you no longer keep the temple a temple; you destroy it. "If anyone among you thinks he is wise" is aimed at those who are struck and harmed by outside learning, for by saying "among you" he marked them off.

Those who have been instructed, who have received the word of knowledge into themselves and have not been shaken from the teaching, he calls temples of the Holy Spirit and unshakable houses of the Spirit who has come to dwell in them. Those who have done something worthy of the Spirit's working he calls spiritual, just as we call people orators and craftsmen when they have given a display of their oratory and their craft. So those who take in a different teaching drawn from outside wisdom have ruined their own reasoning, debasing the faith, the Spirit's temple, like counterfeit coin. That is why he threatens that God will destroy them: they left the Teacher who dwells in them and wandered off after outside wisdom, which is well able to supply deceit.
On 1 Corinthians 3:21–23: Having charged them not to accept outside wisdom, he teaches them not to boast in wise men either…

added_allusions.reason: 'as in Ezekiel': the watchman who must warn sinners; no words quoted, so not cited inline.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The False Judgment of Disciples
english: …for such boasting is cheap when all things are yours: the apostles (they were sent for the sake of those who would benefit), the world, which came to be for your enjoyment, life, since you are being saved, and death (if death held no terrors, the things of the life to come would not have been preferred to this one). "Things present and things to come" are said on the same principle: those who despise present things as passing obtain the things to come. So all the things he has listed are yours, because you have become Christ's, and those who are made Christ's own are pleasing to God.

The second catena form adds: "All things are yours." How, and in what way? Because you have become Christ's. And to show that those who are made Christ's own are pleasing to God, he added, "and Christ is God's."
On 1 Corinthians 4:1: It is enough for us to be honored as servants of Christ; to have people named after us is offensive.

On 1 Corinthians 4:2: Look on us as servants of God, but do not you inquire which servant is faithful, for that is where your danger lies; and it is not right for teachers to be judged by their pupils. Why does he say this? He was aware that they honored some unworthy teachers and passed over worthy ones, and he foresaw that this would lead to schisms among them. That is why he rebukes them so sharply, hurrying to check the trouble.

On 1 Corinthians 4:3: So that he would not seem to say this out of disdain, as a man who had been slighted, he all but says: Do not think I am sending you this on my own account. I do not live in a way that calls for me to be examined by you. I think that beneath me, where you or any man is concerned. By "a human day" he means human beings, pointing to how passing and short-lived human life is. Then, since "I know nothing against myself" seems a large claim, he added, "but I am not justified by this." For a man can stumble through ignorance without his conscience pricking him. Besides, it is not avoiding evil that justifies; it is achieving virtue that makes a man complete. It is likely, too, that he said this out of restraint: do not think more highly than befits you, but wait for the judge.

On 1 Corinthians 4:5: All the way through he keeps to his aim, bringing to their senses those who wanted to be named after one man and not after another, for that is what people do who sit in judgment on who is worthy and who is not. So do not think more highly than befits you, but wait for the judge. A put-on character can deceive you, but nothing hidden could escape the one who brings to light the hidden things of darkness. He said this because much among them went on by deceit, and unworthy men were honored. Those who were honored were not wholly good; they held to virtue only for show, while those who were good in their nature were passed over. Otherwise he would not have said this.

On 1 Corinthians 4:6: He brings forward himself and Apollos and keeps silent about the names of those who demanded honor and wanted the disciples named after them, so that you may take from us a pattern and an example for treating teachers with moderation. Do not think of us beyond what is written, but regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1), and do not dishonor some teachers while honoring others. Here he exposed their attitude more plainly: whoever was named after one man and slighted another was puffed up on the first man's behalf and turned his conceit against the second.

On 1 Corinthians 4:7: You who want to be called after this man or to drop that one, who judges you? Are you not waiting for the judge? You, whose part is to obey, are waiting for the judge, and yet you put your teacher under your own judgment?

The second catena form adds: And you, a layman, who judges you for what you think or do, that you dare to judge others, and teachers at that? Is it not the Lord? If you, the disciple, wait for the Lord as judge, how can you put your teacher under your own judgment, calling one worthy and another unworthy?

Why do you think you have an advantage that you neither have nor have received? He means the surpassing intelligence that would let a person judge and test even teachers. Even if you received your understanding from God, you must give the glory to God who gave it, not think great things of yourself and be lifted up, putting it forward as an advantage of your own.

On 1 Corinthians 4:8: Not that things really stood so with them; he shows that this was their state of mind. They held false opinions of themselves and thought they had been filled with all knowledge, to the point of judging even their teachers. Already the gifts have become a surfeit to you, and you no longer long for them. "Without us" means: before we reigned, you got there first and reigned. And by setting "would that you did reign" in between…

title: The Purpose of Paul's Visit and Correction
english: …he shows how he himself feels. Then, by saying "so that we too might reign with you," he makes plain that he counts their successes as blessings of his own. It is reasonable, too, to read "you have reigned" and "you have become rich" as questions, so that the words carry the same tone as "Already you are filled."

On 1 Corinthians 4:9: As I see it, if you have become rich and have reigned without us, then we who have endured everything have become the last of all, men condemned to death. "To men," he says, because they see our sufferings, "and to angels," because they marvel at our steadfastness.

On 1 Corinthians 4:10: These words are of the same kind. Those who teach you live in contempt and poverty, so that the world even takes them for fools, while you who are taught want to be already in wealth and in the honors of Christ. He says this to show that in spiritual gifts "a disciple is not above his teacher" (Matthew 10:24).

On 1 Corinthians 4:11–13: We endure everything for Christ's sake, and to this day we humble ourselves. How then can you, living in the flesh, be preferred before God to those who toil, are persecuted, are reviled and are beaten? Through all this he teaches what a Christian must be like, and how he must humble himself. That is, scrapings. We have become like the sweepings and the dung carried out of a house that has been cleaned, despised by everyone, and we are the refuse of all, putting ourselves beneath everyone for Christ's sake. And "offscouring" is the word for the towel that wipes the sweat off a laborer and rubs away the grime that clings to him.

On 1 Corinthians 4:14: Having attacked them hard in the earlier words, he comforts them with these, so that by mixing the astringent with the sweet he may make up a medicine with the power to save. "Shaming" means putting to confusion.

On 1 Corinthians 4:15: By calling himself their father, and the men they were named after their tutors, he shows that his affection for them is truer than the others', and that, since a father is the one warning them, they ought not to take offense.
On 1 Corinthians 4:16: Become imitators of me by not looking down on anyone or being lifted up, and by being called after no one but Christ.

On 1 Corinthians 4:18–20: You see that what he said earlier, "We are weak, but you are strong," and all the rest, was said because some had become puffed up and proud. "But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power." In these words he rebukes them strongly, and by threatening to come in person he himself bears witness that they can still be set right. He announces his coming as if to see whether they will show themselves humbled, and corrects them by his word before he comes. Yet he added "if the Lord wills." Indignation drove him to say "I will come," but reverence reminded him to add that finest of additions, "if the Lord wills." Here he brings into the open what he had said earlier in veiled terms, so as not to seem to rebuke them too harshly: "for the kingdom of God is not in word," meaning polished speech, since the apostles did not teach and preach without words.

The second catena form adds: He announces his coming so that they may set themselves right before he arrives. It becomes clearer from this that his anger is aimed at those who boast in the wisdom of this world, for he does not mean to discredit ordinary speech; and this he proclaimed to them too, for all to hear.

On 1 Corinthians 4:21: Correction comes in two forms: by admonition for those who will listen, and by force and compulsion for the stiff-necked. In his kindness he left the choice between them to the Corinthians, so that they might repent and set themselves right. By "rod" he meant the compelling power of the Spirit, which Paul used against Elymas (Acts 13:8–11), and which God used against Paul himself (Acts 9:3–9).

On 1 Corinthians 5:1–5: They were puffed up, not because that man had a woman in the way described, but because he was eloquent. They did not mourn that he had his father's wife; they were proud that he was well educated. Their mourning would either have cut the fornicator off if he persisted, or driven the outrage out and brought him back. Not simply "who did" but "who has carried out": he did not fall because he was swept away; he made the evil his deliberate work. And he says that he is present in spirit, casting his vote with them and joining in the condemnation (by "spirit" he means…
